analysis.one_liner: Bars federal agencies from issuing job-affecting rules and blocks any tax increase for two years.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had a single sponsor and no cosponsors, never left committee and received no vote before the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: For two years, no federal agency could issue any rule that would affect employment levels — a test nearly every significant rule on wages, workplace safety, or benefits could meet — and Congress could not pass any law that raised anyone's taxes, including taxes on the highest earners and largest corporations. The bill was referred to three House committees, got a subcommittee referral in one, and then went nowhere.
analysis.who_benefits: Regulated industries and high-income households. A two-year freeze on any rule that touches employment would block new wage, overtime, workplace-safety, and benefit protections, and the flat ban on any tax increase would shield the wealthiest people and largest companies from any new tax.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits every federal agency from making any rule that would affect employment levels for two years after enactment.
Bars Congress from enacting any law that would result in an increase in the tax liability of any person or entity.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary workers and consumers. Rules that protect pay, safety on the job, benefits, and consumer protections routinely affect employment levels and would be blocked, and any revenue measure — including one aimed only at top earners — would be off the table.

drawbacks.text: Because virtually any significant federal rule can be argued to affect employment levels, the two-year moratorium could sweep in wage rules, workplace-safety standards, and benefit regulations, leaving workers without new protections for the period.
The blanket ban on any increase in tax liability for any person or entity applies to the wealthiest households and largest corporations, not just to small businesses or middle-class families.

Proponents could argue the freeze reduces regulatory uncertainty for employers in a weak job market, and that it is limited to two years — but the definition of 'affect employment levels' is so broad that the cost to worker protections would likely far outweigh that benefit.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is speculative and short-lived: two years of reduced regulatory uncertainty for employers. The cost is concrete: a near-total freeze on new employment-related rules and a blanket shield against any tax increase, which mostly protects concentrated wealth. The bill is also poorly designed — the employment-effects test is so broad that it would be nearly unenforceable in any limited way.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in three House committees after referral, got a subcommittee referral in Judiciary, and died there when the Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Rep. Mike Rogers of Michigan introduced the bill on November 29, 2011, with no cosponsors.
It was referred to the Ways and Means, Oversight and Government Reform, and Judiciary Committees; no markup or floor action ever occurred.
The only further action was a referral to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Courts, Commercial and Administrative Law on December 5, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained a new advantage; ordinary workers simply avoided a two-year freeze on wage, safety, and benefit rules and a blanket ban on tax increases.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Ordinary people, since the freeze never happened

for.name: Rep. Mike J. Rogers
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to three committees; it drew no cosponsors.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for markup or floor action after referral.

against.name: House Judiciary Subcommittee on Courts, Commercial and Administrative Law
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on December 5, 2011 and took no further action.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had one Republican sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party, and no votes were ever taken, so no partisan divide showed up in the record.

industries.note: A two-year freeze on any rule affecting employment levels would block new wage, overtime, workplace-safety, and benefit regulations. The industry's gain would come directly at the cost of workers' protections.
The flat ban on any tax increase for any person or entity would shield top earners and the largest companies from any new tax for two years.
The moratorium would prevent agencies from issuing rules on wages, benefits, and job safety that unions and worker advocates push for.
